# Introduction

Although ANOVA and MANOVA share extreme similarities, it doesn't just mean that one has more dimensions than the other. There are many misconceptions on the applications of each analysis. While they share similar outputs, they can mean completely different outcomes. In addition, many researchers may want to conduct ANOVA after running a MANOVA onto their data. This can lead to an inflated Type II Error, damaging the overall analysis.

This paper will run both ANOVA and MANOVA onto a dataset presented by the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository. The dataset "Wine Quality" [@paulo_cortez_wine_2009] includes red and white wine quality characteristics such as acidity, pH, sugar, chlorides, density, etc. We will apply the two different tests to see if any of these variables have different means between different quality groups. Each quality group is determined by the score of the wine. These groups are low (scores 3-4), medium (scores 5-6) and high (scores 7-8). Scores of 1,2,9, and 10 have minimal to no data within this dataset so they will disregarded within these groups.

The key difference between ANOVA and MANOVA is that MANOVA includes multiple continuous dependent variables that are test simultaneously. MANOVA can calculate whether at least one or a combination of variables have a significant difference between groups. MANOVA will prevent false positives also known as Type 1 Errors from increasing in contrast to running many singular ANOVA tests.

In this paper, we will see that both MANOVA and 11 ANOVA tests result with significantly small p-values. MANOVA tells us that at least one or a combination of variables has a significant difference between wine quality groups. Each ANOVA test will specifically state whether the independent variable alone has a significant difference between quality groups. As said previously, running 11 ANOVA tests will increase our false positive rates. In addition, ANOVA tests will only tell us if the singular variable alone has a significant difference. In some scenarios, ANOVA may not result in any significant results while MANOVA does. MANOVA can detect whether combinations of variables can differ between groups unlike ANOVA. Lastly, we will discuss different MANOVA methods that could improve this study, as there are many assumption corrections we will stumble upon.

# Data

The data is provided by the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository called “Wine Quality”. [@paulo_cortez_wine_2009] Each observation is from a Portuguese varietal of both red and white wine called the “Vinho Verde” wine. Each wine will have a score from 0 to 10 indicating a wine’s overall quality. There are 4898 observations for white wines and 1599 observations for red wines highlighting that there has been more white wines taste tested in contrast to red wines for this varietal. We will be testing our methodology onto white wines.

One thing to note upon is the data collection methods. From the UCI Repository, the data has been collected from various expert taste tests from 2004 to 2007. Each test is certified through the official wine organization in Portugal known as the Comissão de Viticultura da Região dos Vinhos Verdes (CVRVV) [@verde_cvrvv_nodate]. The data does not identify whether each entry was conducted through different people. This can cause an issue with our analysis assumption regarding the independence of observations. If the same expert taste tests two different wines, the expert’s bias may cause a dependency between each observation they submit. 

Each of the wine observations include the following variables:

-   Fixed acidity: The intensity of acids present naturally in wine.

-   Volatile acidity: The intensity of acids present after yeast fermentation.

-   Citric acid: A natural organic acid in wine grapes.

-   Residual sugar: Natural grape sugars.

-   Chlorides: Affects saltiness and mouthfeel

-   Free sulfur dioxide: Unbound sulfur dioxide used as antioxidants.

-   Total sulfur dioxide: The combined concentration of free and bound sulfur dioxide.

-   Density: The overall density/weight of the wine, affects the mouthfeel.

-   pH: The pH of the wine, can change overall taste and acidity levels.

-   Sulphates: A preservation byproduct after fermentation.

-   Alcohol: The alcohol percentage.

-   Quality Score: The final score given from 1 to 10.

After testing for missing or outlier prone data, we found that there exists 200 outliers within this dataset using a 1.5 × IQR boundary calculation with the “rstatix” package. Outliers can increase the variation in groups causing an increase chance of Type II error so we will be proceeding to analyze the data without the outliers.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "The histogram of white wine quality scores showing the frequency of each quality score"

hist(winequality_white$quality, main = "Histogram of White Wine Quality Scores" , xlab = "Quality Score", breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 10, by = 1))

```

By looking at the histogram of the frequency distribution of quality scores, we can see that the overall quality scores are concentrated around 4-6 slightly favoring higher scores like 6 and 7. Minimal data exists around the scores of 1, 2, 9, and 10 so we will disregard those scores for our groups. Although this may significantly increase Type II Error, we will continue with this for the sake to compare the analysis types. The issue of choosing which groups are in which range can be perceived differently by different analysts so in many to all settings, creating groups should be avoided unless there are strict definitions set from the dataset provider. For future improvements, we can dive deeper to understand if there are already set splits defined by an official scoring rule book to avoid Type II Error.

# Methods

In this paper, we will be comparing the application of multiple univariate ANOVA tests and MANOVA. Both tests will be applied to the "groups" of scores. These groups are split among scores such as 3-4, 5-6, and 7-8. These groups are chosen because there will be too little data for wines that score 1,2,9, and 10.

**For ANOVA:**

We will apply ANOVA with each variable looking into each score group. To do so, we will need some assumptions.

Normality:

-   The normality assumption can be bypassed by applying the Central Limit Theorem (CLT). Since each quality group has a sample size above 30, each group's distribution can be assumed to be approximately normal.

Homogeneity of Variance:

-   The homogeneity of variance assumption will be violated in a standard ANOVA. Since each group includes sample sizes with large differences, this test will most likely fail.

-   We can apply Levene's Test [@noauthor_1.3.5.10._nodate] to test the equality of variance for each quality group.

    -   If the Levene's Test fails, we will apply Welch's ANOVA [@discovery_welchs_nodate] which does not require the data to have unequal variances.

    -   Unfortunately, this may introduce a Type II error as we will be "looking" at the data before applying our ANOVA. This can lead to possible false negatives.

    -   So for our overall ANOVA, we will not apply Levene's Test and apply Welch's ANOVA directly without a check.

Independence:

-   The independence assumption will be difficult to prove. As discussed earlier, the UCI Wine Quality Dataset does not state specific observation retrieval methods or list the "expert" who tested each wine. Due to this, we cannot say if each observation is independent to one another. If a single expert has tested multiple wines in our data, then there will be high risk of correlation between those observations.

We can write the model for ANOVA as the following:

$$
X_{lj} = \mu +\tau_l + \epsilon_{lj} 
$$

Where:

-   $X_{lj}$ represents the wine's variable level at each observation (acidity, sugars, pH, etc).

-   $\mu$ represents the overall average of the wine's quality.

-   $\tau_l$ represents each treatment or quality group of the wine.

-   $\epsilon_{lj}$ represents the error for the specific observation. The error is iid(N0, $\sigma^2$).

The test will see if the following null hypothesis is true:

$$
H_0 : \tau_1 = \tau_2 = \tau_3 = 0
$$

Where each treatment group (low,medium,high) is equal to 0.

Our alternative hypothesis will be:

$$
H_a : atleast \ one \ \tau_l  \ne 0
$$

Where each at least one group (low,medium,high) is not equal to 0.

**For MANOVA:**

The MANOVA tests include both the Normality and Independence assumption similar to the univariate ANOVA tests. However, the MANOVA requires the variance-covariance matrix to be equal across groups instead of just variances. In addition, MANOVA requires that each variable has a slight multicollinearity.

Homogeneity of Variances:

-   A similar issues arise to MANOVA as each group has larges differences between sample sizes. Due to this, we cannot apply a standard MANOVA to this dataset.

Correlations within variables:

-   @fig-corr shows the correlation matrix between each variable highlighting that there exists slight correlations between each variable ranging from 0.02 to 0.84. For future tests, it may be better to isolate extremely low and high correlation variables and test those variables in a univariate ANOVA. However, since we are comparing the two different tests, we will proceed with MANOVA and not increase Type II error risk.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-corr
#| fig-cap: "The correlation matrix between each variable"
wine_corr_df <- winequality_white[,c("fixed acidity", "volatile acidity", "citric acid", "residual sugar", "chlorides", "free sulfur dioxide", "total sulfur dioxide",
  "density", "pH", "sulphates","alcohol")]
wine_corr_matrix <- cor(wine_corr_df)

ggcorrplot(wine_corr_matrix, 
           hc.order = TRUE,        # Clusters similar variables together
           type = "lower",         # Cleans clutter by showing only bottom half
           lab = TRUE,             # Overlays the actual correlation numbers
           lab_size = 2, 
           colors = c("#64C4FF", "white", "#FF7F7F")) +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1))
```

For this paper, we will proceed to apply a standard MANOVA test even though the assumption is violated to understand the comparison to univariate ANOVA tests. We expect MANOVA to tell us that there exists at least either a singular or combination of variables that differs between quality groups. We expect the singular ANOVA tests to tell us directly whether each individual variable differs between quality groups. If MANOVA identifies a difference and the ANOVAs do not, then there exists at least one joint combination of variables that is significantly different between groups and that each individual variable does not matter independently.

We can write the model for MANOVA as the following:

$$
X_{lj} = \mu +\tau_l + \epsilon_{lj}
$$

Where:

-   $X_{lj}$ represents a vector of wine's variable level at each observation (acidity, sugars, pH, etc). This can also be any combinations of the variables as well.

-   $\mu$ represents the overall average of the wine's quality.

-   $\tau_l$ represents each treatment or quality group of the wine.

-   $\epsilon_{lj}$ represents the error for the specific observation. The errors are independent $N_p(0, \sigma^2)$

The test will see if the following null hypothesis is true:

$$
H_0 : \tau_1 = \tau_2 = \tau_3 = 0
$$

Where each treatment group (low,medium,high) is equal to 0.

Our alternative hypothesis will be:

$$
H_a : atleast \ one \ \tau_l  \ne 0
$$

Where each at least one group (low,medium,high) is not equal to 0.

For future improvements, we can apply different MANOVA techniques similar to Welch's ANOVA such as MANOVA.RM. [@friedrich_manova.rm:_2026]

# Results

After conducting both MANOVA and multiple Welch's ANOVAs, we can notice multiple things. With MANOVA, our output results a p-value of 2.2e-16. This means that there exists at least one dependent variable that differs between between two or more quality groups. The MANOVA's output will not tell us which variable has this significant difference. For example, the output does not tell us if fixed acidity is significantly different or if a combination of variables is significantly different. The combination of fixed acidity, volatile acidity, and citric acid may contribute to a difference between groups but the independent variables may not. To check this, we would need to proceed with individual ANOVA tests.

For our univariate Welch's ANOVAs, our results show that every variable chosen has a significant difference between quality groups. Every p-value shown in @tbl-pval has output values lower than our alpha which is 0.05/11 after applying a Bonferroni Correction with 11 variables. This confirms our previous statement where each individual acidity variable has a significant difference between groups independent from each other.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| label: tbl-pval
#| tbl-pos: "H"
#| tbl-cap: "A table for all 11 p-values for each univariate ANOVA test."

t1 = oneway.test(`fixed acidity` ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

t2 = oneway.test(`volatile acidity` ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

t3 = oneway.test(`citric acid` ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

t4 = oneway.test(`residual sugar` ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

t5 = oneway.test(chlorides ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

t6 = oneway.test(`free sulfur dioxide` ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

t7 = oneway.test(`total sulfur dioxide` ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

t8 = oneway.test(density ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

t9 = oneway.test(pH ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

t10 = oneway.test(sulphates ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

t11 = oneway.test(alcohol ~ quality_group, data = winequality_white, var.equal = FALSE)

tab <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Fixed Acidity", "Volatile", "Citric Acid", "Residual Sugar", "Chlorides", "Free Sulfur Dioxide", "Total Sulfur Dioxide",
           "Density", "pH", "Sulphates","Alcohol"),
  P_Value = c(t1$p.value, t2$p.value, t3$p.value, t4$p.value, t5$p.value, t6$p.value,t7$p.value, t8$p.value, t9$p.value, t10$p.value, t11$p.value)
)

tab2 <- tab
tab2$P_Value <- formatC(tab2$P_Value, format = "e", digits = 4)

kable(tab2, format = "latex", table.envir = "table", align = c('l', 'c'), col.names = c("Variable", "p-value"))


```

# Discussion

In this paper, we found that both MANOVA and ANOVAs results have show significant p-values. For MANOVA, the p-value indicates that there exists at least one variable or a combination of variables that are different between at least 2 wine quality groups. For the 11 ANOVAs, the p-values indicate that all of the variables independently have significantly different values between at least 2 wine quality groups. In addition, the 11 ANOVAs will also increase our Type 1 error rate due to conducting 11 separate tests instead of 1 singular MANOVA. We want to apply MANOVA to tell us if a combination of variables has a significant difference across groups. In contrast, if we want to know if individual variables have different values across groups, then we want to apply individual ANOVAs. I

As said in the methods section, MANOVA's assumptions are not met for this dataset. The data does not include independent variance-covariances violating one of the assumptions for MANOVA. For future tests, we can possibly conduct different types of MANOVA methods such as MANOVA.RM which can help analyze data with unequal variance-covariances across groups. Since neither MANOVA nor ANOVA will provide information for prediction, carrying out multiple linear regression may be beneficial if we want to predict wine quality scores given the variables.
